claim: Heterochromatic gene silencing usually requires specific histone modifications.
source: Heterochromatic gene silencing is an important form of gene regulation that usually requires specific histone modifications.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental support in this manuscript.

claim: A popular model posits that inheritance of modified histones, especially in the form of H3-H4 tetramers, underlies inheritance of heterochromatin.
source: A popular model posits that inheritance of modified histones, especially in the form of H3-H4 tetramers, underlies inheritance of heterochromatin.
evidence: This describes an existing model in the field, supported by citations elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: H3-H4 tetramers are randomly distributed between daughter chromatids during DNA replication.
source: Because H3-H4 tetramers are randomly distributed between daughter chromatids during DNA replication, rare occurrences of asymmetric tetramer inheritance within a heterochromatic domain would have the potential to destabilize heterochromatin.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and is supported by citations to classic studies (Sogo et al., 1986; Cusick et al., 1984) in the manuscript.

claim: Rare occurrences of asymmetric tetramer inheritance within a heterochromatic domain would have the potential to destabilize heterochromatin.
source: Because H3-H4 tetramers are randomly distributed between daughter chromatids during DNA replication, rare occurrences of asymmetric tetramer inheritance within a heterochromatic domain would have the potential to destabilize heterochromatin.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the model that histones carry epigenetic memory.

claim: The model predicts that shorter heterochromatic domains would experience unbalanced tetramer inheritance more frequently, and thereby be less stable.
source: This model makes a prediction that shorter heterochromatic domains would experience unbalanced tetramer inheritance more frequently, and thereby be less stable.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the histone inheritance model through logical inference.

claim: Shortening a heterochromatic domain in Saccharomyces had no impact on the strength of silencing nor its heritability.
source: In contrast to this prediction, we found that shortening a heterochromatic domain in Saccharomyces had no impact on the strength of silencing nor its heritability.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Replisome mutations that disrupt inheritance of H3-H4 tetramers had only minor effects on heterochromatin stability.
source: Additionally, we found that replisome mutations that disrupt inheritance of H3-H4 tetramers had only minor effects on heterochromatin stability.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: Histones carry little or no memory of the heterochromatin state through DNA replication.
source: These findings suggest that histones carry little or no memory of the heterochromatin state through DNA replication.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Faithful transmission of epigenetic information is crucial for multiple heterochromatin-based processes such as X-chromosome inactivation in mammals and cold-induced gene silencing in Arabidopsis.
source: Faithful transmission of epigenetic information is crucial for multiple heterochromatin-based processes such as X-chromosome inactivation in mammals and cold-induced gene silencing in Arabidopsis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The identity of epigenetic information remains unclear and heavily debated.
source: Surprisingly, the identity of this epigenetic information remains unclear and heavily debated.
evidence: This characterizes the current state of the field.

claim: Histone subunits H3 and H4 are marked by a variety of covalent modifications that are integral to heterochromatin function.
source: The histone subunits of nucleosomes, especially histones H3 and H4, are marked by a variety of covalent modifications that are integral to heterochromatin function.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: During DNA replication, nucleosomes are partially disrupted and marked parental H3-H4 tetramers are locally inherited to daughter chromatids.
source: During DNA replication, nucleosomes are partially disrupted and marked parental H3-H4 tetramers are locally inherited to daughter chromatids.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Prior et al., 1980; Jackson, 1988; Schlissel and Rine, 2019.

claim: Parental H3-H4 tetramers are reassembled into nucleosomes that are interspersed with nucleosomes containing newly synthesized H3-H4 tetramers.
source: As these tetramers are inherited, they are reassembled into nucleosomes that are interspersed with nucleosomes containing newly synthesized H3-H4 tetramers (Prior et al., 1980; Jackson, 1988; Schlissel and Rine, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Prior et al., 1980; Jackson, 1988; Schlissel and Rine, 2019.

claim: One model for epigenetic inheritance posits that marked parental histones inherited through DNA replication recruit histone modifiers to deposit similar marks on new adjacent nucleosomes.
source: One model for epigenetic inheritance posits that marked parental histones inherited through DNA replication recruit histone modifiers to deposit similar marks on new adjacent nucleosomes, thereby reestablishing the previous local landscape of histone modifications (Hecht et al., 1995; Hoppe et al., 2002; Gaydos et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes a model supported by citations to Hecht et al., 1995; Hoppe et al., 2002; Gaydos et al., 2014.

claim: The H3K27 methyltransferase PRC2 binds preferentially to H3K27me3 in vitro.
source: In support of this model, the H3K27 methyltransferase PRC2 binds preferentially to H3K27me3 in vitro (Hansen et al., 2008) and some other modifying enzymes show a similar ability to bind their histone modifications (Zhang et al., 2008; Hecht et al., 1995; Imai et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hansen et al., 2008.

claim: Some histone modifying enzymes show an ability to bind their histone modifications.
source: In support of this model, the H3K27 methyltransferase PRC2 binds preferentially to H3K27me3 in vitro (Hansen et al., 2008) and some other modifying enzymes show a similar ability to bind their histone modifications (Zhang et al., 2008; Hecht et al., 1995; Imai et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2008; Hecht et al., 1995; Imai et al., 2000.

claim: In S. pombe, localized methylation of H3K9 can silence a reporter gene, and this silenced state is heritable in the presence of the H3K9 methyltransferase Clr4p as long as the demethylase Epe1p is absent.
source: In S. pombe, localized methylation of H3K9 can silence a reporter gene, and this silenced state is heritable in the presence of the H3K9 methyltransferase Clr4p as long as the demethylase Epe1p is absent (Audergon et al., 2015; Ragunathan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Audergon et al., 2015; Ragunathan et al., 2015.

claim: Induced removal of silencer elements from silenced chromatin in S. cerevisiae causes almost all cells to lose silencing of adjacent genes after just one round of DNA replication.
source: Conversely, induced removal of silencer elements from silenced chromatin in S. cerevisiae causes almost all cells to lose silencing of adjacent genes after just one round of DNA replication (Holmes and Broach, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holmes and Broach, 1996.

claim: Removal of silencers from Drosophila chromatin silenced by the Polycomb complex causes loss of silencing after DNA replication.
source: Similar results are found when silencers are removed from Drosophila chromatin silenced by the Polycomb complex (Laprell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Laprell et al., 2017.

claim: Parental H3-H4 tetramers have long been thought to be randomly partitioned between daughter chromatids.
source: The model in which histones carry epigenetic memory makes a testable prediction: since parental H3-H4 tetramers have long been thought to be randomly partitioned between daughter chromatids (Sogo et al., 1986; Cusick et al., 1984), rare events could occur in which most or all marked parental H3-H4 tetramers within a domain segregate asymmetrically to one daughter chromatid, causing the other to inherit primarily newly synthesized histones.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sogo et al., 1986; Cusick et al., 1984.

claim: A chromatin domain with an insufficient number of marked parental tetramers would be expected to experience a loss-of-chromatin-state event.
source: A chromatin domain with an insufficient number of marked parental tetramers would be expected to experience a loss-of-chromatin-state event.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the histone inheritance model.

claim: A smaller chromatin domain would correspond to fewer marked nucleosomes and yield more frequent events in which parental H3-H4 tetramers segregate asymmetrically and the chromatin state is lost.
source: In this view, a smaller chromatin domain would correspond to fewer marked nucleosomes and yield more frequent events in which parental H3-H4 tetramers segregate asymmetrically and the chromatin state is lost.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the histone inheritance model.

claim: The potential use of domain size for protection against epimutation is widely conjectured.
source: This potential use of domain size for protection against epimutation is widely conjectured (Dodd et al., 2007; Kaufman and Rando, 2010; Moazed, 2011; Ramachandran and Henikoff, 2015), and may explain why chromatin domains subject to stable epigenetic inheritance are often many kilobases long.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dodd et al., 2007; Kaufman and Rando, 2010; Moazed, 2011; Ramachandran and Henikoff, 2015.

claim: Chromatin domains silenced by Polycomb Responsive Elements (PREs) in Drosophila usually extend beyond 10 kb.
source: For example, chromatin domains silenced by Polycomb Responsive Elements (PREs) in Drosophila usually extend beyond 10 kb (Schwartz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwartz et al., 2006.

claim: A chromatin domain containing only three H3K27me3-marked nucleosomes in A. thaliana is inherited more frequently than would be predicted if random segregation of tetramers caused loss events.
source: In contrast, one study in A. thaliana found that a chromatin domain containing only three H3K27me3-marked nucleosomes is inherited more frequently than would be predicted if random segregation of tetramers caused loss events (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: The E and I silencers flanking HMR and HML are occupied by the DNA-binding proteins Rap1, Abf1, and ORC, that collectively recruit Sir proteins.
source: Specifically, the E and I silencers flanking HMR and HML are occupied by the DNA-binding proteins Rap1, Abf1, and ORC, that collectively recruit Sir proteins; Sir1 is present only at silencers, whereas Sir2/3/4 complexes bind to silencers and spread across the locus in a process that requires deacetylation of H4K16 (Rusché et al., 2002; Thurtle and Rine, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rusché et al., 2002; Thurtle and Rine, 2014.

claim: Sir1 is present only at silencers, whereas Sir2/3/4 complexes bind to silencers and spread across the locus in a process that requires deacetylation of H4K16.
source: Specifically, the E and I silencers flanking HMR and HML are occupied by the DNA-binding proteins Rap1, Abf1, and ORC, that collectively recruit Sir proteins; Sir1 is present only at silencers, whereas Sir2/3/4 complexes bind to silencers and spread across the locus in a process that requires deacetylation of H4K16 (Rusché et al., 2002; Thurtle and Rine, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rusché et al., 2002; Thurtle and Rine, 2014.

claim: DNA methylation and RNA interference do not exist in S. cerevisiae.
source: Notably, DNA methylation and RNA interference do not exist in S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is established knowledge about S. cerevisiae.

claim: Under normal conditions, HMR and HML are constitutively silenced.
source: Under normal conditions, HMR and HML are constitutively silenced.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these loci in S. cerevisiae.

claim: Rare and transient loss-of-silencing events at HMR and HML can be measured by a sensitive assay that uses the cre recombinase under control of the HMLα2 promoter to convert transient transcriptional events into permanent, heritable changes in fluorescence phenotypes.
source: Rare and transient loss-of-silencing events can be measured by a sensitive assay that uses the cre recombinase under control of the HMLα2 promoter to convert transient transcriptional events into permanent, heritable changes in fluorescence phenotypes (Dodson and Rine, 2015).
evidence: This describes the CRASH assay, supported by citation to Dodson and Rine, 2015.

claim: Deletion of SIR1 causes genetically identical cells to be in either of two states at HMR and HML: either fully silenced or fully expressed.
source: In contrast, deletion of SIR1 causes genetically identical cells to be in either of two states at HMR and HML: either fully silenced or fully expressed (Pillus and Rine, 1989; Xu et al., 2006; Dodson and Rine, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pillus and Rine, 1989; Xu et al., 2006; Dodson and Rine, 2015.

claim: Different transcriptional states at HMR and HML in sir1∆ cells are mitotically heritable and cells switch between states at a low frequency.
source: These different transcriptional states are mitotically heritable and cells switch between states at a low frequency.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sir1∆ cells, supported by prior citations.

claim: Full-length HMRα::cre contained fourteen well-positioned nucleosomes between the E and I silencers.
source: HMRα::cre contained fourteen well-positioned nucleosomes between the E and I silencers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by MNase-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletions of DNA corresponding to different sets of nucleosomes at HMRα::cre did not affect the local positions of the remaining nucleosomes as measured by MNase-Seq.
source: These deletions did not affect the local positions of the remaining nucleosomes as measured by MNase-Seq (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by MNase-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The silencing-loss rate predicted by random segregation of H3-H4 tetramers would be approximately 0.006% of cell divisions for full-length HMRα::cre (Strain N14).
source: The silencing-loss rate predicted by random segregation of H3-H4 tetramers would be approximately 0.006% of cell divisions for full-length HMRα::cre (Strain N14) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a calculated prediction based on the model, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Full-length HMRα::cre loses silencing in approximately 0.1% of cell divisions.
source: Previous studies demonstrate that this strain loses silencing in approximately 0.1% of cell divisions (Dodson and Rine, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dodson and Rine, 2015.

claim: The smallest allele of HMRα::cre (Strain N7) would be expected to lose silencing in approximately 1% of cell divisions based on random segregation of H3-H4 tetramers.
source: In contrast to the full size HMRα::cre, the smallest allele of HMRα::cre (Strain N7) would be expected to lose silencing in approximately 1% of cell divisions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a calculated prediction based on the model, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Decreasing nucleosome number at HMRα::cre led to a slight decrease in silencing loss as measured by sector frequency.
source: Surprisingly, decreasing nucleosome number at HMRα::cre led to a slight decrease in silencing loss as measured by sector frequency (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Flow cytometry measurements confirmed that nucleosome number did not strongly affect silencing-loss rates at HMRα::cre, and that reduction of nucleosomes might have a slight stabilizing effect on silencing.
source: Using flow cytometry to measure the frequency of cells that contain both RFP and GFP, we confirmed that nucleosome number did not strongly affect silencing-loss rates, and that reduction of nucleosomes might have a slight stabilizing effect on silencing (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Changing nucleosome number at HMLα::cre led to only a small increase in silencing loss, and these effects were not due strictly to domain size.
source: Additionally, we found that changing nucleosome number at HMLα::cre led to only a small increase in silencing loss, and that these effects were not due strictly to domain size (Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5.

claim: The silencers flanking HMRα are bound by three different proteins that collaborate to recruit Sir proteins.
source: The silencers flanking HMRα are bound by three different proteins that collaborate to recruit Sir proteins (Rusche et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rusche et al., 2003.

claim: Sir1 binds to silencers, and deletion of SIR1 partially disrupts silencer activity, as measured by defects in silencing establishment and silencing heritability.
source: Sir1 binds to silencers, and deletion of SIR1 partially disrupts silencer activity, as measured by defects in silencing establishment and silencing heritability (Pillus and Rine, 1989; Dodson and Rine, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pillus and Rine, 1989; Dodson and Rine, 2015.

claim: Within individual cells in a population of sir1∆ cells, HMR is either transcriptionally silenced or fully expressed.
source: Within individual cells in a population of sir1∆ cells, HMR is either transcriptionally silenced or fully expressed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in figures.

claim: In sir1∆ cells, HMRα was silenced in roughly 99% of cells and was expressed in the remaining cells.
source: In comparison to control strains in which HMRα was fully silenced (SIR+) or expressed (sir4∆), HMRα was silenced in roughly 99% of sir1∆ cells and was expressed in the remaining cells (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Live-cell imaging of sir1∆ cells revealed cells in which silencing of HMR was lost, and other cases in which it was gained.
source: We used live-cell imaging to monitor divisions of sir1∆ cells to identify cells in which silencing of HMR was lost, and other cases in which it was gained (Figure 2A, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2A and Video 1.

claim: Full-length HMRα::GFP in sir1∆ contained twelve nucleosomes.
source: Twelve nucleosomes were present in full-length HMRα::GFP (Strain sN12) (JRY11478).
evidence: This is supported by MNase-Seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Nucleosome number did not affect the frequency of silencing loss at HMRα::GFP in sir1∆ as measured by time-lapse microscopy.
source: Using time-lapse fluorescence microscopy to monitor transcriptional states in individual cells and their descendants as they divided, we found that nucleosome number did not affect the frequency of silencing loss (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The frequency of silencing establishment at HMRα::GFP in sir1∆ was similar between strains with different numbers of nucleosomes.
source: The frequency of silencing establishment was similar between strains with different numbers of nucleosomes at HMRα::GFP (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: dpb3∆ causes biased parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance to the lagging strand.
source: Specifically, dpb3∆ causes biased parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance to the lagging strand (Yu et al., 2018) and a set of point mutations in MCM2 (mcm2-3A) causes biased parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance to the leading strand (Petryk et al., 2018; Gan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2018.

claim: mcm2-3A causes biased parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance to the leading strand.
source: Specifically, dpb3∆ causes biased parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance to the lagging strand (Yu et al., 2018) and a set of point mutations in MCM2 (mcm2-3A) causes biased parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance to the leading strand (Petryk et al., 2018; Gan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Petryk et al., 2018; Gan et al., 2018.

claim: Local histone H4 inheritance in a small chromatin domain was moderately reduced in both the dpb3∆ and mcm2-3A single mutants, and severely reduced in the dpb3∆ mcm2-3A double mutant.
source: A complementary study found that local histone H4 inheritance in a small chromatin domain was moderately reduced in both the dpb3∆ and mcm2-3A single mutants, and severely reduced in the dpb3∆ mcm2-3A double mutant (Schlissel and Rine, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schlissel and Rine, 2019.

claim: Dpb3 and Mcm2 are necessary for efficient inheritance of parental H3-H4 tetramers to both daughter chromatids during DNA replication.
source: Together, these studies demonstrate that Dpb3 and Mcm2 are necessary for efficient inheritance of parental H3-H4 tetramers to both daughter chromatids during DNA replication.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited studies.

claim: The dpb3∆ and mcm2-3A single mutants exhibited higher silencing-loss rates at HMRα::cre than wild type.
source: The dpb3∆ and mcm2-3A single mutants exhibited higher silencing-loss rates, consistent with previous studies done at HML (Yu et al., 2018; Gan et al., 2018), and the dpb3∆ mcm2-3A double mutant lost silencing more frequently than either single mutant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The dpb3∆ mcm2-3A double mutant lost silencing at HMRα::cre more frequently than either single mutant.
source: The dpb3∆ and mcm2-3A single mutants exhibited higher silencing-loss rates, consistent with previous studies done at HML (Yu et al., 2018; Gan et al., 2018), and the dpb3∆ mcm2-3A double mutant lost silencing more frequently than either single mutant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Flow cytometry measurements confirmed that dpb3∆ and mcm2-3A mutants had higher silencing-loss rates at HMRα::cre.
source: Similar results were obtained by using flow cytometry to measure silencing-loss rates (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Epigenetic information that determines expression states in sir1∆ is transmitted locally at HML and HMR, respectively, rather than being transmitted in trans from processes elsewhere in the cell.
source: Testing this possibility was important because the currently unidentified epigenetic information that determines expression states in sir1∆ is transmitted locally at HML and HMR, respectively, rather than being transmitted in trans from processes elsewhere in the cell (Xu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2006.

claim: Populations of dpb3∆, mcm2-3A, and dpb3∆ mcm2-3A mutants in sir1∆ background all showed a mix of cells that were silenced or expressed at HMRα::GFP.
source: Populations of dpb3∆, mcm2-3A, and dpb3∆ mcm2-3A mutants all showed a mix of cells that were silenced or expressed at HMRα::GFP; all three mutant strains also showed a higher frequency of expressed cells than wild type (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Table 1.

claim: All three replisome mutant strains (dpb3∆, mcm2-3A, and dpb3∆ mcm2-3A) in sir1∆ background showed a higher frequency of expressed cells at HMRα::GFP than wild type.
source: Populations of dpb3∆, mcm2-3A, and dpb3∆ mcm2-3A mutants all showed a mix of cells that were silenced or expressed at HMRα::GFP; all three mutant strains also showed a higher frequency of expressed cells than wild type (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Table 1.

claim: dpb3∆ and mcm2-3A in sir1∆ background had higher loss-of-silencing rates at HMRα::GFP than wild type as measured by FACS.
source: By using these relaxation rates to calculate silencing-loss rates (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), we observed that dpb3∆ and mcm2-3A had higher loss-of-silencing rates than wild type (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and Figure 4C.

claim: The dpb3∆ mcm2-3A double mutant in sir1∆ background had a higher loss-of-silencing rate at HMRα::GFP than the single mutants as measured by FACS.
source: The dpb3∆ mcm2-3A double mutant had a higher loss rate than the single mutants.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Similar loss-of-silencing trends were observed using time-lapse fluorescence microscopy, albeit with overall higher loss rates than those seen with FACS.
source: Similar loss trends were observed using time-lapse fluorescence microscopy (Figure 4D), albeit with overall higher loss rates than those seen with FACS.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The vast majority of silenced cells in replisome mutant backgrounds still faithfully transmitted the silenced state.
source: However, we also noted that the vast majority of silenced cells still faithfully transmitted the silenced state in the replisome mutant backgrounds.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Any strain containing dpb3∆ in sir1∆ background had an increased establishment rate at HMRα::GFP.
source: Curiously, any strain containing dpb3∆ had an increased establishment rate, whereas mcm2-3A had minimal, if any, effects on establishment rate (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E–G.

claim: mcm2-3A in sir1∆ background had minimal, if any, effects on establishment rate at HMRα::GFP.
source: Curiously, any strain containing dpb3∆ had an increased establishment rate, whereas mcm2-3A had minimal, if any, effects on establishment rate (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E–G.

claim: Any strain containing dpb3∆ in sir1∆ background showed elevated levels of HMRα::GFP expression in unsilenced cells, as measured by flow cytometry.
source: Additionally, any strain containing dpb3∆ showed elevated levels of HMRα::GFP expression in unsilenced cells, as measured by flow cytometry (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: dpb3∆ and mcm2-3A single mutants exhibit asymmetric parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance.
source: Indeed, though dpb3∆ and mcm2-3A single mutants exhibit asymmetric parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance (Yu et al., 2018; Petryk et al., 2018), it is likely that this asymmetry is not complete and some parental H3-H4 tetramers are still stochastically transmitted to each daughter chromatid during DNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yu et al., 2018; Petryk et al., 2018.

claim: The dpb3∆ mcm2-3A double mutant exhibits residual local inheritance of histone H4.
source: Similarly, the dpb3∆ mcm2-3A double mutant exhibits residual local inheritance of histone H4 (Schlissel and Rine, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schlissel and Rine, 2019.

claim: There was no clear correlation between silencing-loss rates and nucleosome number at HMRα::GFP in dpb3∆ and dpb3∆ mcm2-3A backgrounds in sir1∆.
source: There was no clear correlation between silencing-loss rates and nucleosome number in these sensitized backgrounds (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Establishment-of-silencing rates at HMRα::GFP in replisome mutant backgrounds in sir1∆ were not strongly affected by nucleosome number, though there was a small increase in the establishment rate with fewer nucleosomes in dpb3∆ mcm2-3A.
source: Establishment-of-silencing rates were also not strongly affected, though there was a small increase in the establishment rate with fewer nucleosomes in dpb3∆ mcm2-3A (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Even when parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance was disrupted and the number of parental H3-H4 tetramers available for inheritance at HMR was decreased, cells faithfully transmitted epigenetic transcriptional states.
source: Therefore, even when parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance was disrupted and the number of parental H3-H4 tetramers available for inheritance at HMR was decreased, cells faithfully transmitted epigenetic transcriptional states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Removal of silencers from heterochromatin via induced recombination demonstrates that silencers are necessary for maintenance of the silenced state.
source: Removal of silencers from heterochromatin via induced recombination demonstrates that silencers are necessary for maintenance of the silenced state.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Induced silencer excision from HMR causes rapid loss of silencing in arrested cells.
source: Specifically, induced silencer excision from HMR causes rapid loss of silencing in arrested cells (Cheng and Gartenberg, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cheng and Gartenberg, 2000.

claim: Removal of silencers from chromatin in S. cerevisiae and Drosophila permits maintenance of silencing in arrested cells, but causes loss of silencing once the same cells subsequently complete one or two rounds of DNA replication.
source: Studies at other loci in S. cerevisiae and Drosophila show that removal of silencers permits maintenance of silencing in arrested cells, but causes loss of silencing once the same cells subsequently complete one or two rounds of DNA replication (Holmes and Broach, 1996; Laprell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holmes and Broach, 1996; Laprell et al., 2017.

claim: The presence of modified histones is not sufficient for silencing maintenance or heritability, depending on the example under consideration.
source: Therefore, the presence of modified histones is not sufficient for silencing maintenance or heritability, depending on the example under consideration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited silencer-removal studies.

claim: Epigenetic states of HML and HMR in sir1∆ are a property of the locus rather than the cell, demonstrating that factors that determine these epigenetic states are inherited locally at HML and HMR respectively.
source: Importantly, epigenetic states of HML and HMR in sir1∆ are a property of the locus rather than the cell, demonstrating that factors that determine these epigenetic states are inherited locally at HML and HMR respectively (Xu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2006.

claim: Epigenetic inheritance of transcriptional states in heterochromatin in Arabidopsis demonstrates that the relevant epigenetic information is carried in cis.
source: Similar studies of an epigenetically-inherited heterochromatin state in Arabidopsis also demonstrate that the relevant epigenetic information is carried in cis (Berry et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berry et al., 2015.

claim: Epigenetic inheritance of transcriptional states in heterochromatin is commonly accompanied by the ability to switch stochastically between states, a feature that implies the existence of imperfectly heritable epigenetic information.
source: Additionally, epigenetic inheritance of transcriptional states in heterochromatin is commonly accompanied by the ability to switch stochastically between states, a feature that implies the existence of imperfectly heritable epigenetic information.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about epigenetic systems.

claim: Other cis-acting factors besides modified H3-H4 tetramers determine the epigenetic state of HMR in sir1∆.
source: Though modified H3-H4 tetramers could theoretically be cis-acting, imperfectly heritable units of information, our evidence to the contrary suggests that other cis-acting factors determine the epigenetic state of HMR in sir1∆.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental results.

claim: One possibility is that the silencer complex self-templates by cooperative oligomerization of silencing factors, and that stochastic changes in epigenetic states reflect the formation or dissolution of such a silencer complex.
source: Given the importance of silencers in inheritance of the silenced chromatin state, one possibility is that the silencer complex self-templates by cooperative oligomerization of silencing factors, and that stochastic changes in epigenetic states reflect the formation or dissolution of such a silencer complex.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Chromatin replicated in the presence of cycloheximide, which blocks the synthesis of new histones, produces daughter chromatids with roughly half the number of nucleosomes, and these nucleosomes appear randomly dispersed along both daughter chromatids.
source: For example, chromatin replicated in the presence of cycloheximide, which blocks the synthesis of new histones, produces daughter chromatids with roughly half the number of nucleosomes, and these nucleosomes appear randomly dispersed along both daughter chromatids (Sogo et al., 1986; Cusick et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sogo et al., 1986; Cusick et al., 1984.

claim: Mutations that reduce tetramer inheritance (dpb3∆ and mcm2-3A) increase the frequency of silencing loss at HMR.
source: Using the CRASH and FLAME assays, we found mild but significant increases in HMR silencing-loss rates in both dpb3∆ and mcm2-3A single mutants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The dpb3∆ mcm2-3A double mutant exhibited higher silencing-loss rates at HMR than either of the single mutants.
source: Additionally, the dpb3∆ mcm2-3A double mutant exhibited higher silencing-loss rates than either of the single mutants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Cells with moderate or severe reductions in inheritance of parental H3-H4 tetramers still exhibited efficient inheritance of the silenced state.
source: Considering the variety of histone modifications that parental H3-H4 tetramers can carry through DNA replication, it was striking that cells with moderate or severe reductions in inheritance of parental H3-H4 tetramers still exhibited efficient inheritance of the silenced state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Some parental H3-H4 tetramers are still transmitted to both daughter chromatids in replisome mutant backgrounds.
source: Though replisome mutants exhibit defects in parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance, some tetramers are still transmitted to both daughter chromatids in replisome mutant backgrounds (Yu et al., 2018; Gan et al., 2018; Schlissel and Rine, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yu et al., 2018; Gan et al., 2018; Schlissel and Rine, 2019.

claim: Cells with both reduced parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance and a reduction in the number of tetramers available for inheritance at HMR exhibited a surprisingly robust ability to transmit the silenced state.
source: Therefore, cells with both reduced parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance and a reduction in the number of tetramers available for inheritance at HMR exhibited a surprisingly robust ability to transmit the silenced state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Inheritance of parental H3-H4 tetramers has little or no impact on epigenetic inheritance of the silenced state of HMR.
source: These data strongly suggested that inheritance of parental H3-H4 tetramers has little or no impact on epigenetic inheritance of the silenced state of HMR.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data.

claim: The expressed state of HMR in sir1∆ cells is formally an epigenetic state: it is heritable through cell divisions and can stochastically switch to the silenced state.
source: The expressed state of HMR in sir1∆ cells is formally an epigenetic state: it is heritable through cell divisions and can stochastically switch to the silenced state.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Histone modifications associated with active transcription can be transmitted through DNA replication.
source: Histone modifications associated with active transcription can be transmitted through DNA replication (Alabert et al., 2015; Reverón-Gómez et al., 2018) and multiple transcription factors can bind to the histone modifications they generate (Jacobson et al., 2000; Owen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alabert et al., 2015; Reverón-Gómez et al., 2018.

claim: Multiple transcription factors can bind to the histone modifications they generate.
source: Histone modifications associated with active transcription can be transmitted through DNA replication (Alabert et al., 2015; Reverón-Gómez et al., 2018) and multiple transcription factors can bind to the histone modifications they generate (Jacobson et al., 2000; Owen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jacobson et al., 2000; Owen et al., 2000.

claim: A model that incorporates positive feedback loops between histone modifications and both silencing machinery and transcription factors, along with parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance, generates robust bistable chromatin states.
source: Indeed, a model that incorporates these positive feedback loops and parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance generates robust bistable chromatin states (Dodd et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dodd et al., 2007.

claim: A model incorporating positive feedback loops and parental H3-H4 tetramer inheritance predicts that random segregation of parental H3-H4 tetramers would lead to loss-of-chromatin-state events, and that decreasing chromatin domain size would also decrease the heritability of both the expressed and silenced states.
source: This model also predicts that random segregation of parental H3-H4 tetramers would lead to loss-of-chromatin-state events, and that decreasing chromatin domain size would also decrease the heritability of both the expressed and silenced states.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model described in Dodd et al., 2007.

claim: Shorter versions of HMR did not strongly affect inheritance of the expressed state of HMR.
source: However, we found that shorter versions of HMR did not strongly affect inheritance of the expressed state of HMR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: dpb3∆ exhibited a ~3-fold increase in the rate of silencing establishment at HMRα::GFP in sir1∆.
source: Curiously, dpb3∆ exhibited a ~3-fold increase in the rate of silencing establishment and mcm2-3A had no observable effect (see Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: mcm2-3A had no observable effect on the rate of silencing establishment at HMRα::GFP in sir1∆.
source: Curiously, dpb3∆ exhibited a ~3-fold increase in the rate of silencing establishment and mcm2-3A had no observable effect (see Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: dpb3∆ but not mcm2-3A led to elevated levels of GFP expression when HMRα::GFP was fully expressed.
source: It is also important to note that dpb3∆ but not mcm2-3A led to elevated levels of GFP expression when HMRα::GFP was fully expressed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Recruitment of the transcriptional activator Ppr1 to HMR causes both increased transcription in expressed cells and an increased establishment rate in sir1∆.
source: However, recruitment of the transcriptional activator Ppr1 to HMR causes both increased transcription in expressed cells and an increased establishment rate in sir1∆ (Xu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2006.

claim: The fidelity of H3-H4 tetramer inheritance has minimal consequences for heritability of the silenced state.
source: Together, our results suggested that the fidelity of H3-H4 tetramer inheritance has minimal consequences for heritability of the silenced state and may affect heritability of the expressed state in some contexts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental data.

claim: The fidelity of H3-H4 tetramer inheritance may affect heritability of the expressed state in some contexts.
source: Together, our results suggested that the fidelity of H3-H4 tetramer inheritance has minimal consequences for heritability of the silenced state and may affect heritability of the expressed state in some contexts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, particularly regarding dpb3∆.

claim: The findings raise doubts regarding the model in which histones are significant carriers of epigenetic memory in S. cerevisiae.
source: These findings raised doubts regarding the model in which histones are significant carriers of epigenetic memory in S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.
